facts.statement: The genus Ogygoptynx and its only species, Ogygoptynx wetmorei, were named by Rich and Bohaska in 1976.
facts.quote: The genus Ogygoptynx, its sole species, Ogygoptynx wetmorei, and the family Ogygoptyngidae, were all established by paleontologists Patricia Vickers Rich and David J. Bohaska in 1976

facts.statement: The species was described from a single ankle bone found in Late Paleocene deposits in Colorado, USA.
facts.quote: based on a single tarsometatarsus (ankle bone) recovered from Late Paleocene (Tiffanian) deposits in Colorado, USA

facts.statement: The fossil ankle bone is elongate and slender, looking similar to that of modern barn owls.
facts.quote: The tarsometatarsus displays a mix of primitive and derived characters. It is elongate and slender, superficially resembling the condition in modern Tytonidae (barn owls).

facts.statement: This extinct owl genus lived in North America during the Paleocene epoch.
facts.quote: Ogygoptynx is an extinct monotypic genus of owls from the Paleocene of North America

facts.statement: Ogygoptynx wetmorei is the oldest known owl fossil discovered worldwide.
facts.quote: It is the earliest known owl fossil in the world

facts.statement: Ogygoptynx wetmorei is the only species within the monotypic family Ogygoptyngidae.
facts.quote: Its only species is Ogygoptynx wetmorei and it is the only genus in the family Ogygoptyngidae

facts.statement: The animal lived between 60.9 and 57.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Selandian to Thanetian (60.9 to 57.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: Scientists consider the existence of this species a puzzle regarding early owl evolution.
facts.quote: The existence of Ogygoptynx wetmorei poses an interesting puzzle in the early evolutionary history of owls

facts.statement: Researchers note a contrast between the modern ankle structure of this North American owl and primitive forms found in Europe at the same time.
facts.quote: Its relatively "modern" ankle morphology, appearing in the Late Paleocene of North America, contrasts with the more "primitive" forms known from roughly contemporaneous deposits in Europe

facts.statement: It is debated why similar advanced owls disappear from the North American fossil record for a long time after this species.
facts.quote: Furthermore, similar advanced owls do not reappear in the North American fossil record until much later, creating a significant temporal gap
